stem: This question is about uniformly accelerated motion.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Define displacement, velocity and acceleration, explain the difference between speed and velocity, and state the condition under which the equations of uniformly accelerated motion apply.

points.description: Displacement: distance moved in a specified direction (from a reference point)
Velocity: rate of change of displacement
Acceleration: rate of change of velocity
Speed is a scalar (rate of change of distance, magnitude only); velocity is a vector (has direction)
The equations apply only when the acceleration is constant (uniform) in magnitude and direction, in a straight line

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Displacement is the distance moved in a specified direction from a reference point. Velocity is the rate of change of displacement, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Speed is a scalar, the rate of change of distance, while velocity is a vector with a direction. The equations of uniformly accelerated motion apply only when the acceleration is constant in size and direction.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: An object accelerates uniformly from velocity $u$ to velocity $v$ in time $t$. Using a velocity-time graph, derive the equations $v = u + at$ and $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.

points.description: The v-t graph is a straight line from u (at t = 0) to v (at time t)
Its gradient is the acceleration: $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$, which rearranges to $v = u + at$
The displacement is the area under the graph
Area = rectangle $ut$ plus triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times t \times (v - u)$
Substituting $v - u = at$: $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: For uniform acceleration the velocity-time graph is a straight line from $u$ to $v$. Its gradient is the acceleration, $a = (v - u)/t$, so $v = u + at$. The displacement is the area under the line: a rectangle of area $ut$ and a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}t(v - u)$. Since $v - u = at$, the triangle is $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$, so $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: A driver travelling at $28\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ on the Harare–Bulawayo road sees an obstruction. Her reaction time is $0.80\ \text{s}$; the car then decelerates uniformly at $5.6\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Calculate

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the distance travelled during her reaction time, in m;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the braking distance, in m;

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: the time taken to brake to rest, in s.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at $14\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from a point $1.6\ \text{m}$ above the ground and is not caught. Air resistance is negligible; $g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Calculate

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the greatest height of the ball above the ground, in m;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the time from release until it hits the ground, in s;

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: its speed as it hits the ground, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

explanation: Definitions and the derivation from gradient and area; then stopping distance $22.400000000000002 + 70.0\ \text{m}$ and a vertical throw reaching $11.6\ \text{m}$ and landing after $2.96\ \text{s}$.
hints: Gradient of v-t = a; area = s.
Constant speed during the reaction time.
Take upwards as positive: the ground is at s = −1.6 m.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Define linear momentum and impulse, state the principle of conservation of momentum, and distinguish between an elastic and an inelastic collision.

points.description: Linear momentum: product of mass and velocity (a vector)
Impulse: force × time for which it acts (= change in momentum)
Principle: total momentum of a system is constant
… provided no resultant external force acts
Elastic: total kinetic energy conserved; inelastic: kinetic energy not conserved (some transferred to other forms), momentum conserved in both

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Linear momentum is the product of an object's mass and velocity. Impulse is the product of a force and the time for which it acts, equal to the change in momentum. The principle of conservation of momentum states that the total momentum of a system remains constant provided no resultant external force acts on it. In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy is conserved; in an inelastic collision some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms, although momentum is still conserved.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Two bodies A and B collide. Use Newton's second and third laws to show that their total momentum is conserved, stating any assumption.

points.description: Third law: force of A on B is equal and opposite to force of B on A (F_AB = −F_BA)
The forces act for the same time Δt
Second law: force = rate of change of momentum, so F_AB Δt = Δp_B and F_BA Δt = Δp_A
Hence Δp_B = −Δp_A, i.e. Δp_A + Δp_B = 0
So the total momentum is unchanged; assumption: no external force acts (closed system)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: By Newton's third law the force exerted by A on B is equal and opposite to the force exerted by B on A, and both act for the same time Δt. By the second law each force equals the rate of change of momentum of the body it acts on, so Δp_B = F Δt and Δp_A = −F Δt. Adding, Δp_A + Δp_B = 0: the momentum gained by one body is lost by the other and the total is constant, assuming no external force acts on the system.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: On a level air track, glider P ($0.30\ \text{kg}$) moving at $0.70\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ collides elastically and head-on with a stationary glider Q ($0.20\ \text{kg}$). Calculate

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the velocity of Q after the collision, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$;
parts.explanation: Momentum: $0.21 = 0.30v_P + 0.20v_Q$. Elastic: $0.70 = v_Q - v_P$. Solving: $v_Q = 0.84\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Momentum: $0.21 = 0.30v_P + 0.20v_Q$. Elastic: $0.70 = v_Q - v_P$. Solving: $v_Q = 0.84\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the velocity of P after the collision, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$;

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: the total kinetic energy after the collision, in J.
parts.explanation: $\tfrac{1}{2}(0.30)(0.14)^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}(0.20)(0.84)^2 = 0.074\ \text{J}$, the same as before ($\tfrac{1}{2}(0.30)(0.70)^2$), as expected for an elastic collision.
parts.workedSolution: 1. $\tfrac{1}{2}(0.30)(0.14)^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}(0.20)(0.84)^2 = 0.074\ \text{J}$, the same as before ($\tfrac{1}{2}(0.30)(0.70)^2$), as expected for an elastic collision.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the force on a wall from a horizontal jet of water that strikes it at $2.2\ \text{kg s}^{-1}$ and $7.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and does not bounce back, in N;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the speed of a $0.058\ \text{kg}$ ball, initially at rest, after it is struck by a racket whose force on it rises steadily from zero to $520\ \text{N}$ and falls steadily back to zero during a contact time of $4.0\ \text{ms}$, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.explanation: Impulse $=$ area of the triangle $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 520 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-3} = 1.0\ \text{N s}$; $v = 1.0/0.058 = 17.9\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Impulse $=$ area of the triangle $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 520 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-3} = 1.0\ \text{N s}$; $v = 1.0/0.058 = 17.9\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

explanation: Elastic collision: $v_Q = 0.84$, $v_P = 0.14\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ with kinetic energy conserved; jet force 16.5 N; impulse 1.0 N s gives $17.9\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
hints: Use momentum and relative speeds together for the elastic collision.
Impulse = area under the force-time graph.

stem: This question is about forces and motion.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State Newton's three laws of motion.

points.description: First law: a body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity
… unless acted on by a resultant (external) force
Second law: the resultant force is equal to (proportional to) the rate of change of momentum (F = ma for constant mass)
… and acts in the direction of the change in momentum (acceleration)
Third law: if body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts a force on A that is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
… and of the same type (the forces act on different bodies)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: First law: a body stays at rest or continues to move with constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it. Second law: the resultant force on a body is equal to its rate of change of momentum (F = ma for constant mass) and acts in the direction of that change. Third law: if body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts on A a force that is equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and of the same type.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: A raindrop falls from rest through still air. Explain why it reaches a terminal velocity.

points.description: At first (speed zero) there is no air resistance, so the only force is the weight and a = g
As the speed increases, the air resistance (drag) increases
So the resultant force (weight − drag) and hence the acceleration decrease
When drag equals weight the resultant force is zero, acceleration is zero and the velocity stays constant (terminal velocity)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: On release the raindrop's speed is zero, so there is no drag and it accelerates at g under its weight. As it speeds up the drag increases, so the resultant force, weight minus drag, decreases and the acceleration falls. Eventually the drag equals the weight; the resultant force is zero, so the acceleration is zero and the drop falls at a constant terminal velocity.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: A lift and its passengers have a total mass of $900\ \text{kg}$. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Calculate

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the tension in the cable when the lift accelerates upwards at $1.4\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, in N;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the tension when the lift, still moving upwards, slows down at $0.70\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, in N;

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: the force from the floor on a $60\ \text{kg}$ passenger during the acceleration in (i), in N.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: A child pulls a $40\ \text{kg}$ sledge across level ground with a rope at $25^\circ$ above the horizontal. The tension is $140\ \text{N}$ and the friction on the sledge is $95\ \text{N}$. Calculate

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the horizontal component of the tension, in N;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the acceleration of the sledge, in $\text{m s}^{-2}$;

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: the normal contact force of the ground on the sledge, in N.

explanation: Laws stated in full; terminal velocity from drag rising to equal weight; lift tensions 10100 N and 8200 N; sledge acceleration $0.797\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ with normal force 333 N.
hints: For the lift, write T − mg = ma with the sign of a.
Resolve the rope tension horizontally and vertically.
